subject: one vs. two latent variables - biological/statistical interpretation?

messages.author: 21500bbcaab21afc
messages.subject: one vs. two latent variables - biological/statistical interpretation?
parts:
Dear group members,

I would like to ask for your opinion regarding the interpretation of two different SEMs.

I have behavioural and morphological traits (measured), and would like to test whether these 2 group of traits are linked. I start with the (well-based) assumption that the traits belonging to a certain group (i.e. behaviour or morphology) would be more tightly associated with each other compared to traits across the two groups.

In my first SEM, I have;

a first latent variable ("behavioural type") is represented by 5 indicator variables, which are different behavioural traits, and

a second latent variable ("morphological type") is represented by 5 indicator variables, which are different morphological traits.

These two latent variables are linked by the inclusion of a (residual) correlation between them, so I can test the relationship between these two group of traits.

Now, if I would build another SEM, this time with a single latent variable, that is represented by all 10 indicator variables (i.e. 5  behavioural and 5 morphological traits), how should I think about the differences between these two SEMs? What I am (biologically/statistically) testing here that is different than in my first SEM?

Just to add as a detail: my first SEM is well-supported by the data, whereas the second one is not.

Sorry for potentially triggering the "hypothesis-driven SEMs only" folks. I am just trying to understand the biological meaning of certain SEM structures.

Cheers,
Ned

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: one vs. two latent variables - biological/statistical interpretation?
parts: how should I think about the differences between these two SEMs? What I am (biologically/statistically) testing here that is different than in my first SEM?

The single-factor model quite literally represents the hypothesis that there is a single factor.  It is statistically equivalent to a 2-factor model in which the factor correlation is fixed to 1, so relative to the 2-factor model, you could interpret this as "behavior and morphology are the same variable".
